To address these questions, we designed an experimental task in which participants completed 30 trials with free choice to use AI assistance (chatbot or automatic answer selection) or respond independently.
Three hundred and ninety eight students (ages 18-24 years) were recruited from the Clemson University (n = 260) and United States Military Academy (USMA; n = 138) research pools.
All participants were 18 years of age or older.

Written informed consent to participate in the research was obtained electronically from every participant before any study procedure began; participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, their right to withdraw at any time without penalty, and that anonymized data could be reported in scientific publications.

Participants completed a measure of a personality trait likely to affect AI use, Need for Cognition (Cacioppo et al., 1984), and four scales assessing attitudes and perceptions toward automation and AI: the Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (Grassini, 2023), the Negative Attitudes toward Robots Scale adapted for AI (Nomura et al., 2006), the Perfect Automation Schema Scale (Merritt et al., 2015), and the Complacency Potential Rating Scale (Singh et al., 1993).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Objective: Research on student AI use typically asks who adopts these tools, treating use as a stable trait.
Yet students face a fresh decision at every problem.
We examined how much AI use reflects stable individual differences and how much varies within a student across tasks.
Method: Undergraduates (N = 398) at two institutions completed 30 quiz trials, choosing on each trial to answer independently, consult an AI chatbot, or rely on an AI-generated answer.
Students rated their topic expertise before each decision; cognitive abilities, AI attitudes, and demographics were also measured.
Choices were analyzed with Bayesian multilevel multinomial logistic regression.

Results: With moderately reliable AI, about half the variance in AI use reflected stable individual differences (intraclass correlations of 41% for chatbot use, 48% for full reliance); the remainder varied within individuals across trials.
Self-assessed expertise accounted for this within-person variation: students sought help primarily when they felt unknowledgeable.
Fluid intelligence predicted more chatbot consultation but less full delegation.
Male students and those with more favorable AI attitudes delegated more readily.
Conclusions: AI use is better described as adaptive help-seeking than as a fixed trait.
Interventions targeting metacognitive calibration may prove more effective than blanket policies assuming uniform use.
The integration of artificial intelligence systems into educational environments has accelerated dramatically in recent years (Kasneci et al., 2023; Zawacki-Richter et al., 2019).

Emerging evidence reveals that even among adopters, trust in AI, which affects reliance, varies across systems and contexts (Glikson & Woolley, 2020).

text.text: Each time a student encounters a problem, they face a choice: attempt it independently or request AI assistance.
This framing draws on classic help-seeking theory, intelligent tutoring systems research, and recent work on generative AI, reviewed below.
Early research in help-seeking treated it as a sign of dependence or immaturity.

Nelson-Le Gall (1985) reframed it as an adaptive learning strategy, describing a sequence of decisions a learner must make: recognizing that help is needed, deciding to seek it, identifying a suitable source, eliciting the help, and evaluating the results.

text.text: Ineffective help-seeking could be caused by a failure at any of those steps. Nelson-Le Gall (1985) also distinguished two kinds of help-seeking based on the goal.

text.text: In instrumental help-seeking, the learner seeks only as much help as is needed, aiming to acquire the understanding needed to solve the problem independently.

In executive help-seeking, the learner has little interest in understanding the solution and aims to have the problem solved by someone else. Newman (2002) later described adaptive help-seeking as a component of selfregulated learning that depends on cognitive competencies, including knowing when help is needed, and on motivational resources such as a willingness to acknowledge difficulty.

text.text: The first of these competencies is metacognitive: learners must monitor their own knowledge accurately to recognize when help is warranted.

Empirical work in this area has mainly focused on the level of person rather than decision. Karabenick (2003), for example, surveyed 883 college students and used cluster analysis to identify groups with distinct help-seeking profiles.

text.text: Strategic, adaptive help-seekers, who relied on instructors were more motivated, held stronger mastery goals, and earned higher grades than students who either avoided help or sought it quickly.
These person-focused findings show that help-seeking tendencies differ reliably between students, but not how the same student decides, problem-by-problem, whether help is worth seeking.
Intelligent tutoring systems made help-seeking behavior more easily observable, because each request is logged with the problem-solving step that prompted it.

In a review of help use in interactive learning environments, Aleven et al. (2003) found that learners frequently used ondemand help ineffectively, avoiding it when it would be useful or overusing it when it is not needed.

text.text: The review found appropriate help use likely to be an interaction between metacognitive skill, cognitive factors such as prior knowledge, and features of the system itself.

Regarding overuse, Baker et al. (2004) studied the most extreme form, termed gaming the system, or systematically exploiting a tutor's hints and feedback, for example by requesting hints in rapid succession until the answer is revealed.

text.text: In classroom observations of a cognitive tutor, gaming was associated with reduced learning, and students who gamed frequently scored substantially lower on a post-test even after controlling for prior knowledge.
However, effective help-seeking can also be taught. Roll et al. (2011) added a Help Tutor that gave immediate feedback on help-seeking errors.

text.text: Across two classroom studies it improved students' help-seeking behavior, and in the second study, which added explicit help-seeking instruction and support for self-assessment, the improved help-seeking skills transferred to new material after the support had been removed.

Generative AI extends the student's help-seeking decision to almost every academic task. Sheese et al. (2024) analyzed more than 2,500 queries that students submitted to a programming assistant, built on a large language model and designed not to reveal complete solutions, and found that students who were more successful in the course tended to use the tool more often. Sung and Thomas (2025) showed that the classic help-seeking framework applies to generative AI: in a survey of university students, general academic help-seeking goals mediated the relationships between achievement goals and ChatGPT-specific help-seeking outcomes, including executive use of ChatGPT, perceived threat, and avoidance.

text.text: The distinction between instrumental and executive help maps onto the choice that generative AI now offers.
A student can interactively consult a chatbot, reading and evaluating its explanation, and following up before committing to an answer, or can have the AI simply supply the answer.
The first resembles instrumental help-seeking and the second executive helpseeking, and the present study offered both options on every trial.
Across this literature, however, help-seeking has been characterized mainly at the person-level.
Whether a given student's decision to use AI help reflects a stable disposition or a judgment made problem by problem has not been examined.
Framing AI use as help-seeking implies that it should vary within individuals across tasks.
Each use decision is made in response to a specific problem under specific conditions, making within-person variation central to understanding AI use behavior.
As a result, classifying students simply as AI "users" or "non-users" provides limited insight into when assistance is actually sought.

Despite this implication, most empirical work on generative AI in education has operationalized AI use as a between-person phenomenon, focusing on overall adoption rates or average use frequency (Strzelecki, 2024).
text.formatted: Despite this implication, most empirical work on generative AI in education has operationalized AI use as a between-person phenomenon, focusing on overall adoption rates or average use frequency <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Strzelecki, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches conflate stable individual differences with situational influences and obscure the processes that govern moment-to-moment AI helpseeking.
Without explicitly separating within-person and between-person sources of variance, it is unclear whether observed predictors reflect enduring propensities or context-sensitive responses.
Distinguishing these levels of analysis is essential for both theory and practice.

If AI use is primarily trait-driven, interventions should target learner characteristics and attitudes; if it is primarily context-dependent, task design and instructional structure become the primary levers.
Addressing this distinction requires research designs that capture repeated AI use decisions within individuals and analytic approaches that explicitly partition variance across levels.
Despite growing interest in generative AI use in educational contexts, existing empirical approaches are poorly suited to examining AI use as a within-person decision process.
Crosssectional surveys cannot capture how decisions to seek AI assistance vary across tasks, nor can between-person associations be used to infer within-person processes (Curran & Bauer, 2011).
text.formatted: Crosssectional surveys cannot capture how decisions to seek AI assistance vary across tasks, nor can between-person associations be used to infer within-person processes <ref type="bibr">(Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Field and quasi-experimental studies improve ecological validity but typically manipulate access to AI assistance or assign AI use experimentally (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026; Noy & Zhang, 2023).

text.text: These designs are well suited for estimating average treatment effects but eliminate learner choice, thereby obscuring the decision-making process central to help-seeking.

Research on intelligent tutoring systems and AI assistants has observed help-seeking behavior directly (Aleven et al., 2003; Sheese et al., 2024) but, as reviewed above, has primarily emphasized between-person differences rather than decomposing trial-level fluctuations within individuals.

text.text: As a result, existing estimates of individual difference effects in AI use may be confounded with situational variation (Curran & Bauer, 2011).

text.text: Addressing these limitations requires a controlled experimental paradigm with repeated decision opportunities in which participants freely choose whether to seek AI assistance.
Such designs sacrifice some ecological validity but enable decomposition of within-person and between-person variance while holding task characteristics and AI reliability constant.
The present study adopted this approach to address two research questions.

From an instructional standpoint, understanding when students seek AI assistance is critical because most AI policies and learning environment practices implicitly assume that AI use is stable across tasks, rather than dynamically regulated in response to task-specific demands.
Treating AI use as a dynamic help-seeking process, we now turn to the specific factors that may shape these decisions.
Table 1 summarizes candidate predictors organized by their expected level of operation, though these assignments are tentative given the absence of prior multilevel research on generative AI use.

text.text: Several predictors likely operate primarily at the between-person level, creating stable propensities toward more or less AI use across contexts.

Cognitive abilities present competing theoretical predictions: higher fluid intelligence, working memory, and attention control could either increase AI use (by enabling better evaluation and integration of AI outputs) or decrease it (by reducing perceived need for external assistance).
Evidence from cognitive offloading research is mixed.

Higher short-term memory capacity predicted less offloading in one study (Meyerhoff et al., 2021), whereas working memory capacity was unrelated to offloading in another (Morrison & Richmond, 2020). Gilbert et al. (2020) found that people with poorer unaided memory used reminders more, and that reminder use beyond the optimal level was predicted by underconfidence relative to actual ability.

text.text: Although help-seeking theory suggests that ability may relate differently to instrumental AI help (consulting a chatbot) than to executive AI help (delegating the answer), none of the prior studies measured fluid intelligence.

Dispositional attitudes toward AI similarly create baseline adoption propensities, with constructs such as perceived usefulness, AI anxiety, and propensity to trust all linked to technology engagement (Davis, 1989; Grassini, 2023; Russo et al., 2025).

text.text: Gender differences in AI adoption are well documented, with women showing lower adoption rates even when access is equalized (Humlum & Vestergaard, 2025; Otis et al., 2024).

text.text: Women also report higher AI anxiety and lower self-assessed AI knowledge (Russo et al., 2025), and self-assessed knowledge explained most of the gap in one large U.S. survey (Aldasoro et al., 2024).

text.text: Other predictors may drive within-person dynamics.
Trial-level metacognitive judgments of self-expertise may trigger AI help-seeking on a moment-to-moment basis.
When individuals perceive a knowledge gap, they are more likely to seek help (Aleven et al., 2003; Undorf et al., 2021).
text.formatted: When individuals perceive a knowledge gap, they are more likely to seek help <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Aleven et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Undorf et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, we expected more AI use on trials where students judge their expertise insufficient.

Still other factors may moderate within-person effects: dispositional trust might amplify or attenuate how strongly self-expertise judgments influence use decisions, with miscalibrated trust producing maladaptive patterns of automation bias or algorithm aversion (Dietvorst et al., 2015; Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010).

text.text: Given these uncertainties about the direction and level of operation of each predictor, and the absence of prior multilevel evidence in generative AI contexts, we adopted an exploratory approach and addressed two research questions.
The first asked to what extent students' AI use was driven by stable individual differences versus factors that vary across tasks (RQ1).
The second asked how trial-level contextual factors related to moment-to-moment use decisions after accounting for individual differences (RQ2).

To address these questions, we designed an experimental task in which participants completed 30 trials with free choice to use AI assistance (chatbot or automatic answer selection) or respond independently.
We assessed both stable individual differences and trial-level psychological states across repeated decision contexts.
This design enabled multilevel analysis of both stable individual differences reflecting adoption propensities and trial-level decisions reflecting contextual variation within persons.

text.text: Three hundred and ninety eight students (ages 18-24 years) were recruited from the Clemson University (n = 260) and United States Military Academy (USMA; n = 138) research pools.
All students received course credit for their participation.
All participants were 18 years of age or older.

Written informed consent to participate in the research was obtained electronically from every participant before any study procedure began; participants were informed of the purpose of the study, the voluntary nature of participation, their right to withdraw at any time without penalty, and that anonymized data could be reported in scientific publications.

text.text: The 18-item Need for Cognition scale was rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (extremely uncharacteristic of me) to 5 (extremely characteristic of me; e.g., "I would prefer complex to simple problems") and scored as a total.

The four-item Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale (e.g., "I believe that AI will improve my life") was rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), modified from the original 10-point format, and scored as a total.
The 14-item Negative Attitudes toward Robots Scale was adapted by replacing "robots" with "AI" in each item and was rated on a 5-point scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Understanding when students seek AI help requires examining both who is predisposed to use these tools and what momentary factors trigger assistance-seeking.
We designed an experimental paradigm to disentangle these levels of analysis.
Given the exploratory nature of the present analyses, the patterns observed here should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
The unconditional model revealed that approximately half of the variance in AI use decisions resided at the between-person level (ICCs of 41% for chatbot choice, 48% for reliance).
This finding suggests that AI use should be conceptualized as a dynamic process shaped by both the situation and trait-like characteristics.
Among between-person predictors, fluid intelligence showed opposing effects across AI use types: higher fluid intelligence predicted increased chatbot consultation but decreased full reliance.
This dissociation parallels the distinction between instrumental and executive helpseeking (Nelson-Le Gall, 1985).

text.text: Consulting the chatbot is most similar to instrumental help, since the student evaluates an explanation and still selects the answer while delegating resembles executive help.
Students higher in fluid intelligence appear to favor the instrumental form, perhaps because they are better able to evaluate a chatbot's reasoning, a possibility our data cannot test directly.

text.text: The specificity of this gender effect to full delegation rather than interactive use suggests that previously documented gaps may reflect comfort with ceding control rather than reluctance to engage with AI tools.
Trial-level self-assessed expertise was a strong predictor across all models.
Participants were substantially less likely to seek AI assistance when they reported topic familiarity (58% reduction for chatbot, 70% for reliance).
This finding supports conceptualizing AI use as helpseeking behavior (Karabenick, 2003; Nelson-Le Gall, 1985).
text.formatted: This finding supports conceptualizing AI use as helpseeking behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Karabenick, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Nelson-Le Gall, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Students appear to monitor their knowledge before each decision and seek help when they judge a gap, as students do in intelligent tutoring systems (Aleven et al., 2003; Undorf et al., 2021).

text.text: One caveat is that self-rated expertise likely also reflects actual knowledge; students who know more may simply answer manually more often without evaluating each question.

Separating the two would require controlling for objective knowledge (cf. Gilbert et al., 2020), which our design does not allow because accuracy was observed only on the subset of questions students chose to answer manually.

text.text: Thus, the expertise effect shows that AI use tracks students' judgments of their own knowledge, whether those judgments reflect metacognitive monitoring, actual knowledge, or both.
Designs with forced unaided trials could separate these accounts.
Chatbot use declined over trials while automation reliance remained stable.

This asymmetry suggests that students may have learned to calibrate their interactive AI use based on experience with the system (Lee & See, 2004), while full reliance reflects a more stable orientation toward automation dependence.
text.formatted: This asymmetry suggests that students may have learned to calibrate their interactive AI use based on experience with the system <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Lee & See, 2004)</ref>, while full reliance reflects a more stable orientation toward automation dependence.

text.text: This pattern implies that interactive consultation and full reliance may invoke different trust and reliance processes (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010).
text.formatted: This pattern implies that interactive consultation and full reliance may invoke different trust and reliance processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, students may have grown less willing to invest the additional effort required by chatbot interaction, preferring instead to simply delegate.

Our data cannot distinguish between these explanations, but the distinction has a practical implication: if chatbot decline reflects appropriate trust calibration, it represents adaptive learning; if it reflects effort minimization, it may signal disengagement.
Future work tracking response quality across trials could distinguish these accounts.
Alternatively, because questions appeared in the same order for all participants, trial position is confounded with item content, and the decline may partly reflect the questions presented later.
Several predictors did not emerge as meaningful in our models.
Working memory, attention control, and Need for Cognition were unrelated to AI use.
Deciding when to seek help may not be cognitively demanding, or these abilities may matter for how well AI is used once sought, which we did not measure.
Negative attitudes toward AI and complacency potential also did not predict use.
Positive attitudes toward AI mattered but general wariness did not.
These findings extend help-seeking theory (Karabenick, 2003; Newman, 2002) to generative AI contexts.
text.formatted: These findings extend help-seeking theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Karabenick, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Newman, 2002)</ref> to generative AI contexts.

text.text: AI assistance removes many social barriers to help-seeking, yet metacognitive processes governing when assistance is needed still apply.
Students did not use AI indiscriminately; instead, they sought it on questions they judged unfamiliar, consistent with metacognitively guided help-seeking.
The dissociation between interactive chatbot use and full reliance also suggests that the instrumental and executive distinction extends from human helpers to AI.

Early evidence suggests that generative AI can improve learning when it supports productive back-and-forth but may impair it when it substitutes for the student's own thinking (Weidlich et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Early evidence suggests that generative AI can improve learning when it supports productive back-and-forth but may impair it when it substitutes for the student's own thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Weidlich et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This pattern has another implication: students were most likely to seek AI help, and especially to delegate, on questions they judged unfamiliar, which are the questions on which they could least evaluate the AI's output. Pak et al. (2026) called this undetected delegation failure: errors go unnoticed because users lack the knowledge to verify (in contrast to traditional complacency, which arises from a lapse in vigilance).

(2026)</ref> called this undetected delegation failure: errors go unnoticed because users lack the knowledge to verify (in contrast to traditional complacency, which arises from a lapse in vigilance).

text.text: Seeking help when knowledge is insufficient is adaptive, but with a fallible AI it concentrates reliance where errors are least likely to be caught.
The problem is worse for full delegation, which removes even the chance to evaluate the AI's reasoning.
Thus, interventions should target not only when students seek help but also their ability to evaluate it.
The substantial within-person variance (52-59%) challenges the premise underlying many institutional AI policies.

Blanket bans or universal permissions assume AI use is a stable student characteristic, yet our findings suggest the same student may appropriately avoid AI on familiar material and appropriately seek it on unfamiliar material within a single assignment.
The strong predictive role of self-expertise judgments points toward a specific intervention target: metacognitive calibration.
Rather than focusing on whether students use AI, educators might focus on whether students accurately recognize when they need help.
Embedding low-stakes knowledge checks or confidence prompts before AI access could promote deliberate decisions rather than habitual use or avoidance.
This approach treats AI as analogous to other learning resources where the goal is strategic deployment rather than abstinence.

Practically, this might involve prompting students to judge their own knowledge before accessing AI assistance, since inaccurate self-evaluations lead students to stop studying prematurely (Dunlosky & Rawson, 2012).
text.formatted: Practically, this might involve prompting students to judge their own knowledge before accessing AI assistance, since inaccurate self-evaluations lead students to stop studying prematurely <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dunlosky & Rawson, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Learning management systems could prompt students to rate their confidence before AI access is granted.
Such interventions target the judgment of one's own knowledge that, in our data, most strongly predicted each use decision.
The dissociation between chatbot use and full delegation also suggests that these behaviors warrant different pedagogical responses.
Interactive chatbot use, which declined over trials and was associated with higher cognitive ability, may represent a form of active learning amenable to instructional scaffolding.

Full reliance, which remained stable and was predicted by attitudes rather than ability, may instead require interventions addressing students' beliefs about automation or their willingness to engage effortfully with difficult material.

Policies that prohibit all AI use may sacrifice the learning benefits of strategic help-seeking, while policies that permit unrestricted access provide no guidance for students who default to delegation.
Instead, policies could specify the times where AI consultation is permitted.
For example, instructors might permit AI use during initial exploration of a topic but require independent work on summative assessments or allow chatbot interaction but not full delegation.
As AI tools become more capable, the question of when to seek assistance will only grow in importance.
Developing students' capacity to make these judgments wisely may prove more durable than any specific policy governing a particular tool.
Our controlled paradigm differs from naturalistic AI use, which involves open-ended assignments, iterative dialogue, variable reliability, and social dynamics around appropriate use.
However, laboratory studies aim to test whether theorized processes can occur under controlled conditions rather than generalize directly to real-world settings (Mook, 1983).
text.formatted: However, laboratory studies aim to test whether theorized processes can occur under controlled conditions rather than generalize directly to real-world settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Mook, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Existing observational studies cannot determine when and why individuals freely choose AI assistance because they either assign AI use or confound task characteristics with use decisions.
Our paradigm enabled the variance to be partitioned by holding difficulty, domain, and AI accuracy constant and allowing participants to choose the response mode on every trial.
Naturalistic research examining whether these predictors operate similarly in graded coursework and extended projects represents the logical next step.
Additionally, our simulated chatbot with a fixed 70% accuracy rate may not capture how students interact with commercial AI systems whose reliability varies across queries and topical domains.

We set accuracy at 70% because automation below roughly this level tends to impair rather than aid performance (Wickens & Dixon, 2007), and because moderate reliability likely reflects what students encounter.
text.formatted: We set accuracy at 70% because automation below roughly this level tends to impair rather than aid performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Wickens & Dixon, 2007)</ref>, and because moderate reliability likely reflects what students encounter.

text.text: Chatbot accuracy varies widely by task: current models exceed 70% on standard multiple-choice benchmarks (OpenAI, 2023), yet GPT-4 fabricated 28.6% of references when replicating systematic review searches (Chelli et al., 2024), and more than half of ChatGPT's answers to programming questions contained errors (Kabir et al., 2024).

text.text: Frontier models answered fewer than 40% of challenging factual questions correctly (Wei et al., 2024), and reliability is uneven across tasks in ways users cannot easily anticipate (Dell'Acqua et al., 2026).

text.text: Even at 70%, the AI simulated in this study was far more accurate than unaided students on these questions (39%; Section 2.4), so deferring to AI was beneficial on average but not on questions a student knew.
However, our use of 70% reliability places limits on the generalizability of our central result.
A current model would likely answer our questions more accurately, and a near-ceiling AI gives little reason to weigh one's own knowledge on each trial, making use more uniform and trait-like.
The roughly equal split between within-and betweenperson variance is thus specific to a moderately reliable AI (such as the one used here).
Future research should vary AI reliability systematically and examine how students adjust their helpseeking as they learn a system's strengths and limitations (Lee & See, 2004).

Each trial began with a question and four response options (Figure 1).
Participants first rated their topic familiarity on a visual analog scale (Step 1), similar to confidence judgments used in metacognitive research on help seeking (Undorf et al., 2021).
They then selected a response mode (Step 2): "use AI" to consult a chatbot before answering (Step 3a), "have AI answer for me" for automatic submission (Step 3b), or "answer manually" (Step 3c).

The chatbot interface simulated real-time generation by displaying responses word-by-word with variable delays (50-120 ms between words), though responses were pre-generated using ChatGPT and Claude to ensure consistency.
AI accuracy was set at 70%, with errors presenting plausible but incorrect information.
This level ensured that relying on the AI would not become the predominant strategy (see Section 4.4).
Feedback appeared for 1500 ms before the next trial (Step 4).
